content: 1. Post-exposure prophylaxis is available and can be used in cases where exposure to SARS-CoV-2 is considered prolonged, particularly during aerosol-generating procedures. 2. The contact tracing period for asymptomatic individuals who test positive for SARS-CoV-2 has been shortened from 10 days prior to specimen collection to 2 days. This change was made to address practical and operational considerations for case investigation and contact tracing programs. 3. Recent data indicate that asymptomatic individuals may have a lower viral burden at the time of diagnosis compared to symptomatic individuals. Consequently, a longer contact elicitation window (10 days) may have limited utility in identifying new COVID-19 cases. 4. The recommendation for a shorter contact elicitation window (2 days) aims to optimize the use of resources for case investigation and contact tracing, focusing on activities most likely to interrupt ongoing transmission. 5. This revised time period aligns with recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO), the European CDC, and Public Health Canada. 6. Routine vaccinations can still be administered to patients if an in-person visit is already scheduled for another purpose and the preventive service can be delivered without additional risk. Alternatively, if the patient and clinician agree that the benefits outweigh the risks of SARS-CoV-2 exposure, vaccinations may proceed. 7. When caring for pregnant patients with known or suspected COVID-19, healthcare providers should use respirators (or face masks if respirators are unavailable), eye protection, gloves, and gowns. 8. Healthcare providers living with individuals at higher risk of severe COVID-19 illness do not need to take additional precautions beyond standard infection prevention measures. Optional personal practices, such as removing work clothing and showering upon returning home, may be considered but lack sufficient evidence of effectiveness. 9. Individuals at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19 should follow general precautions, including frequent handwashing, maintaining physical distance (6 feet or about two arm lengths), avoiding sick individuals, and cleaning/disinfecting frequently touched surfaces. 10. Pregnant healthcare workers can work with potentially infected COVID-19 patients, as current data do not suggest an increased risk of severe illness during pregnancy. However, pregnant women have historically been at higher risk of severe illness from other respiratory viruses, such as influenza. 11. Healthcare providers with underlying health conditions should adhere to recommended infection prevention and control practices when caring for COVID-19 patients. Facilities may prioritize assigning lower-risk staff to care for COVID-19 patients when feasible. Providers concerned about their individual risk should discuss this with their supervisor or occupational health services. 12. People aged 65 and older, as well as those with serious underlying health conditions (e.g., heart disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes), are at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19. 13. Healthcare providers suspecting a patient has COVID-19 should immediately notify their facility’s infection control personnel. Positive test results must be reported to local or state health departments. 14. Patients with asthma, particularly those with moderate to severe or poorly controlled asthma, may be at higher risk of severe illness from COVID-19. However, current guidelines for asthma management remain unchanged. 15. Continuation of inhaled corticosteroids is critical for asthma patients, as there is no evidence of increased COVID-19 morbidity with their use, and they help reduce the risk of asthma exacerbations. 16. Asthma patients without COVID-19 symptoms or diagnosis should continue necessary nebulizer treatments. 17. The CDC recommends eye protection for healthcare providers in areas with moderate to substantial community transmission of COVID-19. In areas with minimal or no transmission, eye protection is optional unless required by standard precautions. 18. COVID-19 Surge is a spreadsheet-based tool designed to help hospital administrators and public health officials estimate the demand for hospital-based services during the pandemic. It provides estimates for hospitalizations, ICU care, and ventilator support, which can be compared to existing or expanded hospital capacity. 19. The estimates generated by COVID-19 Surge are not predictions but are intended to assist in planning and preparing for potential surges in demand. Users can modify input values to reflect their jurisdiction’s situation and explore various scenarios. 20. The FDA has approved COVID-19 blood tests to measure antibody levels in individuals.
